I encountered some rendering errors in tmux/v/3.7a.

For some reason, my mise/Config/mise.toml/Global/Lockfile had pinned tmux to 3.7a, and mise upgrade tmux / mise upgrade tmux --bump both kept reporting "up to date" even after 3.7b was out — see mise/Config/mise.toml/Global/Lockfile for why.
yazi and Lazygit opened to a blank pane inside tmux, but rendered immediately in a plain Ghostty window outside tmux.
Entering tmux copy-mode and leaving it again made the UI suddenly appear — the frame had been drawn the whole time, tmux just never flushed it to the client.
3.7 added tmux support for synchronized-output escape sequences (DECSET 2026), which yazi and lazygit use to paint a full frame atomically.

3.7a's redraw-on-end-of-sync fix was incomplete, so the pane's client redraw wasn't always triggered when the synchronized update ended — the pane just sat on stale content until something else forced a full repaint, like copy-mode.
tmux's CHANGES entry "Fix so that the end of a synchronized update again triggers a redraw" appears for both 3.6b→3.7a and 3.7a→3.7b.
Why this surfaced after removing Nix
tmux had been Nix-managed, pinned below 3.7, predating synchronized-output support entirely.
Why this surfaced after removing Nix
After My/Dotfiles moved tmux to mise with version = "latest", mise resolved that to 3.7a — new enough to hit this bug.
Why this surfaced after removing Nix
Pinned tmux to 3.7b explicitly in mise/Config/mise.toml/Global (~/.config/mise/config.toml), since "latest" couldn't self-heal past the stuck lockfile entry.
Confirmed: yazi and lazygit render immediately inside tmux again, no copy-mode trick needed.

Toggl Track: Time Tracking Software for Any Workflow
Toggl Track Integration Options (Time Entry CRUD Focus)

Below is a comparison of CLI tools, MCP (Model Context Protocol) interfaces, SDKs/libraries, and the official Toggl Track API for performing full Create/Read/Update/Delete (CRUD) on time entries. Each option is noted as official or third-party, whether it's open source, its capabilities (time entry CRUD is mandatory; project/client management and reporting are optional), the required environment/language, and any notable caveats. Longer per-option narrative from the original deep-research run lives on each embedded page under an AI/Response heading that cites this report.
Toggl Track Integration Options (Time Entry CRUD Focus)

Table: eight Toggl Track integration options with time entry CRUD (details live on the embedded pages). "Projects/Clients CRUD" on those pages indicates create/update support where applicable. "Reports" denotes summarized-report capability. Third-party options here are open-source; the official row is the documented REST API.

Aside from the above, there are a few more niche CLI utilities (open-source) for Toggl Track, though with narrower scope or older API versions. For example, toggl-hammer is a Python CLI to quickly add "hour blocks" of time for past dates (useful for back-filling time, but it doesn't let you specify custom start/stop times or descriptions) . It's designed for "lazy" input of fixed-length entries and is not a general-purpose CLI for full CRUD. There are also older CLI projects like joequery/Toggl-CLI and community scripts, but many were built against the now-deprecated API v8. The Toggl Track engineering team maintains a list of third-party tools, and many CLI projects have been updated or forked to work with API v9 . When choosing a CLI, ensure it supports API v9, as the older v8 endpoints are no longer available. The three CLI options above (Python, Node, Rust) are among the best-maintained for Toggl Track with API v9 support and cover a range of language ecosystems. All are open source, allowing you to inspect or modify the code if needed.

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a newer approach that allows AI or natural-language-driven clients (like ChatGPT plugins or Claude AI) to interact with services through a standardized interface. In the Toggl Track context, MCP servers act as an adapter on top of the Toggl API to interpret high-level commands (often in natural language) into Toggl actions. This can be useful if you want to control Toggl via conversational AI or integrate it into an AI agent workflow. Two notable MCP implementations exist for Toggl Track; narrative for each is on Toggl/MCP/Node/louis030195/toggl-mcp and Toggl/MCP/Python/jasleen19/toggl-mcp, under each page's AI/Response heading that cites this report.
SDKs and Libraries for Toggl Track

If you prefer to build your own tools or integrations, there are several software development kits (SDKs) and libraries for Toggl Track. These provide programmatic access to Toggl's API in various languages, abstracting the raw HTTP calls. Below are some of the open-source libraries (and one official, the API itself) that support full time entry CRUD, with notes on projects/clients and reports support:
SDKs and Libraries for Toggl Track

Python: Officially, Toggl Track doesn't maintain an official Python SDK, but the community has the above-mentioned Toggl CLI (Python) Toggl/CLI/Python/AuHau/toggl-cli which doubles as a library. It provides Python classes for TimeEntry, Project, Client, etc., that you can create, fetch, update, and delete in your own scripts . For example, you can do api.TimeEntry(description="New entry", start=..., stop=...).save() to create an entry, or call api.TimeEntry.objects.all() to list entries . Similarly, api.Project.objects.get(id) and .save() let you update project details . This essentially is an SDK built on the Toggl API. Another third-party library, toggl-track (PyPI) by Maurizio Branca, offers a Pythonic interface and CLI; however, it's relatively new (as of 2025) with fewer users . For most Python integrations, using the toggl-cli's API wrapper or simply calling the Toggl REST endpoints via requests (with the official docs) are common approaches.
